prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: B005 is the entry I can defend most easily on the principle that the discovery comes first and the names second. Seven of eight colleagues put it in their top four and three placed it first, and the reasons given are scientific rather than reputational. The magic-wavelength lattice removes the dominant motional and Stark shifts while letting thousands of atoms be interrogated at once, which is a genuine conceptual step and not just better engineering of an existing clock. The result is a clue from nature in my sense: clocks at the 1e-18 level are already used to test the constancy of fundamental constants, to look for ultralight dark-matter couplings, and to resolve the gravitational redshift over millimetres to centimetres, which is general relativity measured in a laboratory. The work is independently reproduced at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL, compared over fibre links, and it is the basis of the planned redefinition of the SI second. Every member who proposed laureates named exactly Katori and Ye, so the attribution is unusually uncontested, with Katori holding the proposal and first realization and Ye the record accuracy and many-body extensions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. Hall and Haensch (2005, the frequency comb) and Wineland (2012, control of single quantum systems, including the ion clock) already cover much of the lineage, and a sceptic can argue that the lattice clock is an extremely well executed step along an already honoured road, and that the committee would be rewarding precision rather than a new phenomenon. A second worry is timing: the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the full practical payoff is still to come, and the cleanest scientific payoff, a measured violation or a variation of a constant, has not been found. A null result that tightens bounds is real science but a quieter story than a new particle or a new state of matter. Finally, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and Derevianko, among others, did key work and cannot be credited under the shortlist's names.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first: a cubic-kilometre detector in Antarctic ice, a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux, then source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane), with Halzen, Karle and Spiering as the plausible three.
responses.response: I share your enthusiasm and ranked B035 second myself, so this is a difference of degree. The discovery is a real clue from nature and the maturity is now adequate. My reservation is attribution. A collaboration of several hundred people delivered the observation, and the line between who conceived the detector and who made the analysis that found the flux is blurrier than the Katori and Ye split. The source evidence from 2018 onward is also still only a few sigma per source, so I want a little more time before I tie a prize to it. I would back B035 as a close alternative, and I would like to hear whether you think Halzen, Karle and Spiering are the right three or whether the committee should ask the outside experts again about the roles within AMANDA and IceCube.

responses.point: Johansson ranks optical-lattice quantum simulation (Bloch, Greiner, Zoller) first as a tunable many-body system with Mott transitions and quantum gas microscopes, and notes Esslinger's omission as an allocation problem.
responses.response: I put B015 eighth, and I should say why, since you place it first. The science is clearly strong and mature, and the Mott transition is a beautiful result. But in my reading the discovery is partly a platform, and its payoff in answering open questions, such as the low-temperature Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram, is still incomplete, so I hesitate to call it a finished discovery. The allocation is also awkward: Zoller and Jaksch for the proposal, Greiner and Bloch for the experiment, and Esslinger left out, which seems to me a real unfairness within the field. That is a weaker position than Katori and Ye, where every colleague agrees on the pair. I do take your point that the work is robustly reproduced, and I would not object to it as a future prize.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the KPZ universality class first as a minimal model organizing growth, directed polymers and random matrices, with experimental checks in liquid-crystal convection, and proposes Kardar and Zhang because Parisi was honoured in 2021.
responses.response: I admire KPZ as a conceptual result and I see why a theorist ranks it first. My problem is the one I raise with all elegant theory: the clean experimental confirmation is thin. The turbulent liquid-crystal experiments confirm the exponents and the Tracy-Widom statistics, but the mathematics has run far ahead of nature, and much of the maturity you describe is exact solution of the model rather than confirmation in a material system. There is also an attribution flaw. The 1986 paper has three authors, and awarding Kardar and Zhang while leaving out Parisi, who was honoured in 2021 for other work, divides one paper's credit in an odd way, and Spohn on the shortlist is a different, later contribution. I would need the outside experts to say that the experimental case is stronger than I think.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the Car-Parrinello method first as a decisive unification of DFT with molecular dynamics that became a standard tool across materials science and chemistry, and ranks the optical lattice clock fourth.
responses.response: The attribution for Car and Parrinello is as clean as for Katori and Ye, and four decades of use is hard to argue with. Where I disagree is on whether it is a discovery in the sense the will asks for. It is a method, and I would want the committee to be clear about the line between a method that enables discoveries and a discovery about nature. Density functional theory and multiscale simulation have already been honoured from the chemistry side, so the area is not untouched. I think optical clocks are different in that they measure nature at a new level and yield a quantity that can be tested against theory. I would, however, accept that physics prizes for instruments and methods have precedent, and I would like to hear how you would phrase a citation that stays clearly inside physics.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should treat the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or fold them into one lineage.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second should be awaited, or whether performance already demonstrated suffices.
Whether Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley or Derevianko have a stronger claim than I credit, which the credited names on the list cannot test.
Whether IceCube attribution can be fixed cleanly among Halzen, Karle and Spiering given the size of the collaboration.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the candidates on this shortlist. My PhD supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet are not credited on any shortlisted ballot, and I have no known tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited names.
